title: Smallest n So 1+2+…+n Is a Multiple of 2024 | AMC 10-Style Level 4

scenes.visual: Running sum 1+2+3+… with a counter. Line 1: counter ticks fast. Line 2: '2024?' badge with a question mark. Line 3: Vantee title card.
lines: Keep adding one plus two plus three. When is the total a multiple of two thousand twenty-four?
Adding it all up would take forever. But a neat trick with neighbors finds it fast.
Hello, I'm Vantee, and today we're hunting for a number!

scenes.visual: Question text with LaTeX 1+2+\cdots+n, read across lines 2–3. Line 4: choice chips 253, 483, 528, 736, 1012.
lines: Find the smallest positive whole number n,
so that one plus two plus three, up to n, is divisible by two thousand twenty-four.
Here are the five choices. Take a good look.

scenes.visual: Line 1: 1+2+⋯+n with 'n' highlighted. Line 2: 'sum ÷ 2024 = whole number', then 'SMALLEST n' marked.
lines: So what do we know? We add every whole number from one to n.
The total must split into groups of two thousand twenty-four exactly. And we want the SMALLEST n.

scenes.visual: Pause card with countdown ring; question and choices visible.
lines: Now it's your turn. Pause the video and give it a go. I'll wait!

scenes.visual: Line 1: two rows: 1, 2, …, n and n, …, 2, 1 under it. Line 2: column pairs glow, each 'n+1', 'n columns'. Line 3: 'sum = n(n+1)/2' (\dfrac).
lines: Welcome back! First, a shortcut for the sum. Write the numbers forward, then backward underneath.
Each column adds to n plus one, and there are n columns.
That counts every number twice, so the sum is half of n times n plus one.

scenes.visual: Rows: '\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2} divisible by 2024' → 'n(n+1) divisible by 4048' → '4048 = 16 × 11 × 23' with factor tiles 16 (green), 11 (purple), 23 (orange); small note '16 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2'.
lines: So half of n times n plus one must be divisible by two thousand twenty-four.
Undo the halving: n times n plus one must be divisible by twice that, four thousand forty-eight.
That's sixteen times eleven times twenty-three. Sixteen is four factors of two; the others are primes.

scenes.visual: Two boxes 'n' and 'n+1' side by side. Line 1: one box tagged 'odd: no 2s'. Line 2: the 16 tile slides whole into the even box. Line 3: an 11 tile tries to sit in both; 'difference = 1' ✗. Line 4: 11 and 23 tiles each drop whole into a box. Line 5: four piles listed: {16,11}|{23}, {16,23}|{11}, {16}|{11,23}, {16,11,23}|{}.
lines: Here's the key. n and n plus one are neighbors, and one of them is odd. It has no factor of two.
So all four factors of two, the whole sixteen, must live in the even one.
Could eleven divide both neighbors? Then it would divide their difference, which is just one.
So eleven goes whole into one neighbor, and so does twenty-three.
We just choose which tiles share a box. That gives four piles to check.

scenes.visual: Pile A: box 16 × 11 = 176. Line 1: both neighbor slots shown (so it doesn't matter which is n). Line 2: 176 with neighbors 175, 177 ✗. Line 3: 352 with 351, 353 ✗. Side strip of multiples of 23 for reference: 161, 184 | 345, 368 | 506, 529. Line 4: 528 with 527 ✗, 529 ✓ and '529 = 23 × 23'. Line 5: 'n = 528, n+1 = 529' pinned as 'best so far' — not yet the final answer badge.
lines: Pile one: sixteen and eleven together, a multiple of one hundred seventy-six. Check both neighbors.
One hundred seventy-six: neither neighbor is a multiple of twenty-three.
Now three hundred fifty-two. No luck again.
Five hundred twenty-eight: its neighbor five hundred twenty-nine is twenty-three times twenty-three!
So five hundred twenty-eight works! Keep it, and check the other piles.
Pile two: sixteen and twenty-three, so three hundred sixty-eight. Neither neighbor has an eleven.
Next, seven hundred thirty-six. Its neighbor seven hundred thirty-seven is eleven times sixty-seven.
It works, but it's bigger than five hundred twenty-eight.

scenes.visual: Pile C: 11 × 23 = 253. Line 2: 253 (252, 254 ✗), 506 (505, 507 ✗); reference multiples of 16: 240, 256 | 496, 512. Line 3: 759 greyed 'past 528, stop'. Line 4: pile D: 4048 greyed. Line 5: answer badge 528, choice C highlighted, chime at END of line.
lines: Pile three: eleven and twenty-three together, a multiple of two hundred fifty-three.
Two hundred fifty-three and five hundred six: none of their neighbors is a multiple of sixteen.
The next is seven hundred fifty-nine, already past five hundred twenty-eight. We can stop.
Pile four: all three together means four thousand forty-eight. Far too big.
So the smallest n is five hundred twenty-eight. That's Choice C!

scenes.visual: Rows per line (\dfrac for the halving): L1 'n(n+1)/2 → halve the even one'. L2 goal tiles '2×2×2, 11, 23'; '253 × 254 / 2 = 253 × 127' odd ✗. L3 '483 × 484 / 2 = 483 × 242', '242 = 2 × 121' (one two) ✗. L4 '528 × 529 / 2 = 264 × 529'. L5 '= (8 × 33) × (23 × 23)', '33 = 3 × 11' ✓. L6 small note 'smallest choice, not yet a proof'.
lines: Faster on test day: check the choices, smallest first, and take half of the even number.
We need eight, eleven and twenty-three. With two hundred fifty-three, the sum is odd!
Four hundred eighty-three times two hundred forty-two has just one factor of two. Not enough!
Five hundred twenty-eight gives two hundred sixty-four times five hundred twenty-nine.
That's eight times three times eleven, times twenty-three times twenty-three. Everything's there!
So five hundred twenty-eight is the smallest CHOICE that works. Solution one proves no n is smaller.
When would you pick this way? On a timed test, with the choices right in front of you.

scenes.visual: Choice chips; wrong ones turn red with a one-line note. L2: '253 = 11 × 23', '2024 = 8 × 11 × 23' with the 8 circled red ('forgot the 8'); sum 253 × 127 is odd. L3: '1012 = 2024 ÷ 2', sum = 506 × 1013, '506 = 2 × 253'. L4: '483 = 21 × 23', '484 = 4 × 121', sum = 483 × 242 → one two. L5: 736 chip amber/green-outlined 'works, but 736 > 528'.
lines: Choice A, two hundred fifty-three, is what you'd get by using just the eleven and twenty-three.
Choice E, one thousand twelve, is half of two thousand twenty-four. Its sum has one factor of two.
Choice B, four hundred eighty-three, has the twenty-three; its neighbor, the eleven. But not the eight!
Choice D, seven hundred thirty-six, really works! But it's pile two's answer, not the SMALLEST.
What is the smallest n so that one plus two, up to n, is divisible by two thousand twenty-five?

scenes.visual: Pause card, countdown, variant question visible.
lines: Pause the video, and go for it!

scenes.visual: L1: 'n(n+1) divisible by 4050'. L2: '4050 = 2 × 81 × 25', '2: free (one neighbor is even)'. L3: tiles 81 and 25; 'both in one: 2025 → n = 2024 or 2025; look for smaller'. L4: walk 81 (80, 82 ✗), 162 (161, 163 ✗), 243 (242, 244 ✗). L5: neighbors marked ✗ (ref: 75, 100 | 150, 175 | 225, 250). L6: 324 (323 ✗, 325 = 25 × 13 ✓). L7: answer badge 324, chime at end of the first sentence; small check row '324 × 325 / 2 = 162 × 325 = 2025 × 26'.
lines: Let's check. Undo the halving: n times n plus one must be divisible by four thousand fifty.
That's two times eighty-one times twenty-five. The two is free, since one neighbor is always even.
Eighty-one and twenty-five each go whole into a neighbor. Both in one is far too big.
So walk the multiples of eighty-one: eighty-one, one hundred sixty-two, two hundred forty-three.
None of their neighbors is a multiple of twenty-five.
Three hundred twenty-four: its neighbor three hundred twenty-five is twenty-five times thirteen!
So n is three hundred twenty-four. If you got it, amazing work!

scenes.visual: Summary card: 'sum = n(n+1)/2 → neighbors share nothing → each prime power goes whole to one neighbor → walk the big multiples'.
lines: Neighbors share no factor bigger than one, so each prime power goes whole into one of them.
Sort the pieces into piles, count up the multiples, and check the neighbors.
I'm Vantee. Keep exploring, and I'll see you next time!
